newsitem.title: GERMANY: Banks blamed for German takeover closecall.
newsitem.headline: Banks blamed for German takeover closecall.

text.p: German trade unions and opposition politicians on Tuesday turned the full force of their anger on the banks which supported a rare, but abortive, hostile takeover bid among Germany's two rival steel producers.

Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp on Monday dropped plans for a bank-financed takeover of Thyssen AG, plans which sparked protests from workers and commentators fearful that Germany's consensus economics were being sacrificed to naked capitalism.

The decision did not pacify 30,000 steelworkers who demonstrated at the headquarters of Deutsche Bank in the financial capital, Frankfurt, with banners reading "Deutsche Bank, executioner of the steelworker".
The firms have agreed to form a steel production joint venture to be managed by Thyssen, and explore other forms of cooperation short of merger.

Thyssen chief executive Dieter Vogel on Tuesday evening said the co-operation solution would provide a better deal for workers than a wholesale takeover and pledged that it and Krupp would endeavour to avoid job shedding.
"The workers would have borne the brunt (of a costly takeover)," Vogel said in a television interview.
The agreement meant Krupp would not have to call on the 15 billion mark credit line it had secured from Deutsche Bank, Dresdner Bank and others.

The banks say they did not instigate the plan but agree they would like to see Germany's steel sector slimmed down to compete with its more efficient British and French rivals -- a process which is still certain to cost thousands of jobs.

Such is the shock to Germany's tradition of consensus among industry, workers, banks and government that the steelworkers have been able to mobilise widespread support among a public increasingly worried by soaring unemployment.

"The banks' machinations are destroying this country's political culture," Klaus Zwickel, the head of the engineering union IG Metall, told the demonstrators who had halted production in the steel plants of Duisburg and Dortmund.
Deutsche has come under particular attack because it had directors on the supervisory boards of both firms, but never told Thyssen that it was supporting a takeover by a rival.
"The parties and the parliament have to ask themselves who it is that rules us -- the democratically elected government or the unchecked finance centres of the big banks," Zwickel said.
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) joined the attack, urging five or 10 percent limits on banks' industrial holdings.
SPD financial expert Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier hailed Krupp's climbdown, saying "one of the decisive factors was that banks had to backtrack in the face of the storm of public protest."

With unemployment now at 4.7 million, a level not seen since 1933, Germany's workers have become increasingly afraid of the restructuring of industry and the welfare state which government and economists say are needed to restore German competitiveness.

Mass protests have become the order of the day, and the steelworkers were following a path beaten this month by miners and construction workers who both wrung money out of Bonn in attempts to save their jobs.
"What's good enough for the miners cannot be too expensive for the steelworkers," Zwickel told the rally, which brought inner-city traffic in Frankfurt to a standstill.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservative Christian Democrats have also had to take account of rising public unease about reforms which to many smack of "Americanisation" -- shorthand for a hire-and-fire culture without a social safety net.

Kohl's powerful lieutenant Wolfgang Schaeuble insisted he opposed such a culture, but told the weekly Die Zeit: "In Germany, even small changes turn into big conflicts. We are more developed than other countries when it comes to defending the status quo...We must not try to pretend we can construct a zone where there will be no conflict."
